title: Be strong (Joshua 1:1–9)
hook: Moses' successor is told three times, "be strong and of good courage"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nevi'im, the Prophets, opening on the day Moses dies. Your line was the story goes on without moses. Today, the first words Joshua hears.

What do you say to someone on the first morning of a job far too big for them? Joshua has just stepped into Moses' place. The book's first verse calls him Moses' minister, his assistant. Now there's a river in front of him, a land of walled cities beyond it, and a whole people watching to see what happens next. God speaks. There's a promise of the land, border to border, but no battle plan, no tactics, no word about the walls. There's one phrase, said, then said again, then a third time. And before the chapter ends, someone says it back to him.
screen: `A JOB TOO BIG.` → `NO BATTLE PLAN.` → `ONE PHRASE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Listen for the repeat. First: be strong and of good courage, because you will lead this people into the land. That one is for the task. Then again, stronger: only be strong and very courageous. And the reason is a surprise. Not to fight. To keep the teaching Moses gave, turning from it neither to the right nor to the left. Then the line: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, but thou shalt meditate therein day and night." The bravest thing asked of the new leader isn't a battle. It's to keep studying, to keep the words in his mouth. Then a third time, with a third reason: be strong and of good courage, don't be afraid, don't be dismayed, "for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." The work, the teaching, and company. Now skip to the end of the chapter. Joshua gives his first orders, and the tribes whose land lies east of the Jordan answer him. Whatever you command, we'll do. Wherever you send us, we'll go. And they close with the very words he was given: only be strong and of good courage. The encouragement that came down to Joshua goes back up to him from the people. So courage here isn't a mood you wait for. It's a command. It can be spoken, repeated and handed on, from God to a leader, and from a crowd to the person in front of it.
screen: `FIRST: FOR THE TASK.` · `SECOND: FOR THE TEACHING, DAY AND NIGHT.` · `THIRD: GOD IS WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE SAY IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Name, quietly, one thing this week that feels too big. Then say be strong, aloud or under your breath, three times: once for the task, once for what you're trying to stay faithful to while you do it, once for the people who are in it with you. If you pray, add the verse's last words: the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Be strong. Chazak, in Hebrew, said to Joshua three times, and then said back to him by the people. Today's word.
Your line: be strong, again. Courage can be handed on, and handed back. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The words chazak ve'ematz, be strong and of good courage, come from Joshua 1, and some say the phrase to encourage someone taking on a new task.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pep talk before a war.
what it means: be strong, said three times with three reasons, the land, the teaching and God's company, and then said back by the people.
what a scholar hears: the strongest form, very courageous, is tied not to battle but to keeping the Torah in your mouth day and night.

chat.says: What did God tell Joshua to be brave about? Just fighting the battles?
options: The task, yes, but also keeping the teaching, and knowing God was with him.
Only the battles; the part about the teaching was meant for the priests.
Ruling well, since Moses had already left him a full plan for the war.
chat.meaning: The charge comes three times: for the task, for keeping the teaching day and night, and because God is with him.

notes: Verify exact JPS 1917 wording of Joshua 1:8 and the end of 1:9.
'Three times' counts God's charge in 1:6, 1:7 and 1:9; the people's echo is 1:18. Confirm the count and that 1:7 reads 'strong and very courageous'.
Day 696 already tied chazak to the end-of-book custom; this day stays in the text of Joshua 1 to avoid repeating it.
howItsDone: the custom of saying chazak ve'ematz to someone taking office is described loosely; a Keeper may refine or cut it.

Editor: cut 'the one standing near the tent' (not in Joshua 1) for 'Moses' minister' (1:1); 'again, louder' became 'again, stronger'; the answering tribes named as those east of the Jordan (1:12–18); howItsDone custom softened to 'some say'.
